result.rule: When the description's opening sentence states an action that a participant performs to start the process (for example, recognising or identifying a situation), and the process then continues with further described work: Model the stated opening action as a task placed after the start event, so that the start event represents the trigger and the task represents the performed work. Do not use the start event label alone to stand for that action, and do not drop the action from the model.

When the description states that an activity runs over a period, that one or more other activities run at the same time while it runs, and that a later step starts only after the period has ended and all of these concurrent activities have finished: Model the concurrent block as parallel branches: place a parallel gateway split before the running activity and the monitoring activity. Model the end of the period as an intermediate catch event (a timer or wait) that is also a branch of the concurrent block. Connect the monitoring activity and the period-end event to a parallel gateway join, so that no branch ends on its own or bypasses the join. Continue from that join to the later step. Do not use an exclusive gateway to merge these branches.

When The description says a later step is triggered only when a time limit or other condition is reached, and it phrases that condition as an event that occurs (for example, that a period ends).: Model the wait as an intermediate catch event, not a task. Name it with the awaited condition in the description's own wording and present tense, so the label states the trigger (for example, 'period ends' rather than the past-tense 'period ended'). Do not add a task whose label restates the same waiting condition.

When the description states that, after a party gives approval or acceptance, the process continues to a named follow-on step, and a later recording or confirmation step depends on that follow-on step: Model the named follow-on step as its own task, placed in the sequence between the approval (an intermediate catch event if it is awaited) and the recording or confirmation step. Do not merge the follow-on step into the approval or into the recording step, and preserve the sequence flows that the description implies.
